etymology: Pass over, the English translation of Hebrew pesach, “to pass over, spare,” from the action of the destroying angel who passed over the houses marked with the blood of the lamb in Egypt (Ex 12). Greek pascha renders the same.
biblical_def: Passover is the foundational redemptive feast of Israel—the annual remembrance of the LORD’s deliverance of His people from Egypt on the night of the tenth plague, when the destroying angel passed over the houses whose lintels and door-posts were marked with the blood of the slain lamb. Exodus 12 prescribes the original observance and its perpetual memorial. The lamb was taken on the tenth day of the first month (Nisan), kept until the fourteenth day, killed in the evening, its blood applied to the door-posts and lintel, its flesh roasted with fire and eaten that same night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, the household clothed and ready for the journey, the meal eaten in haste. For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD. And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt (Ex 12:12-13). The structural features of the doctrine are several. First, the substitution: the lamb died in place of the firstborn; the blood of the lamb stood between the destroying angel and the household marked with it; substitutionary atonement is set out at the very foundation of Israel’s national identity. Second, the appropriation: not all who saw the blood were spared, but those whose households were marked by faith in the LORD’s appointed sign; the blood applied was the means of salvation. Third, the meal: the lamb was eaten by those it had saved; the saved community was constituted by the shared feast on the substitute. Fourth, the perpetual memorial: Passover was to be kept every year as a remembrance and as a teaching ordinance: and it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service? That ye shall say, It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s passover, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, when he smote the Egyptians, and delivered our houses (Ex 12:26-27). Fifth, and supremely, the typological fulfillment in Christ. Paul: for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor 5:7-8). John the Baptist’s announcement: behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29). 1 Peter 1:18-19: redeemed not with corruptible things, as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. The Last Supper, instituted at the Passover meal, became the New Covenant memorial of the substitutionary death of the True Passover Lamb. Christ Himself was crucified at Passover, at the very hour the Passover lambs were being slain in the temple court. The Passover therefore stands at the center of biblical theology: the foundational Old Testament redemptive event prefiguring the once-for-all redemptive death of Christ, whose blood passes over every soul that has been marked by faith in His atoning work.

The paschal lamb was killed on the fourteenth day of Abib (Nisan), and eaten that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

corruption_summary: The Passover doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the supersessionist reading that has treated the Passover as merely a Jewish historical festival superseded and discarded by Christianity (rather than as the foundational shadow whose substance is Christ)—and on the other by certain Messianic and Hebrew-roots movements that have urged Christian observance of the OT Passover as continuing covenantal obligation, against the apostolic teaching that Christ has fulfilled the feast and the Lord’s table is now the New Covenant memorial.
corruption_paragraphs: The supersessionist reading treats the Passover as merely a Jewish historical festival superseded and discarded by Christianity, with little operative connection to Christian doctrine beyond an occasional sermon illustration. The apostolic teaching is sharper. The Passover is the foundational shadow whose substance is Christ; the New Testament writers do not discard the Passover but trace its typological fulfillment in Christ’s death. Christ Himself ate the Passover with His disciples and instituted the Lord’s Supper as the New Covenant memorial in continuity with the Passover’s redemptive substance. The Christian who reads past Passover as merely Old Testament-Jewish detail has missed one of the deepest typological connections in the Bible. The recovery is the recovery of the typology: Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us; the Passover’s every detail prefigured Him; the New Covenant’s Lord’s table preserves the substance the Passover prefigured.

The opposite corruption is the Messianic and Hebrew-roots movements that have urged Christian observance of the OT Passover as continuing covenantal obligation. Some traditions have argued that Christians (Gentile and Jewish believers alike) should annually celebrate Passover in something like its OT form, with a seder, the four cups, the bitter herbs, the unleavened bread, and so on. The apostolic teaching does not warrant this. Christ has fulfilled the Passover; the Lord&rsquo>s Supper instituted at the Last Supper is the New Covenant memorial; the apostolic church across the NT does not observe a continuing Passover separate from the Lord’s table; Paul explicitly rebukes the imposition of Old Covenant feast-keeping on Gentile believers (Gal 4:10; Col 2:16-17, let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ). The Christian celebration of Passover’s substance happens at every observance of the Lord’s Supper; the substance is Christ; the OT Passover is fulfilled. Recover both ends. Refuse the supersessionist reading that discards the Passover as discarded-Jewish-festival, and refuse the imposition of OT Passover observance on Christians whose new covenant memorial is the Lord’s table. The biblical doctrine traces the Passover’s substance through to Christ and finds the New Covenant fulfillment at the bread-and-cup of His own institution.

etymology: From Greek pentēkostē, “fiftieth,” counted from the day after the Passover Sabbath as the fiftieth day of the firstfruits-counting; the OT Feast of Weeks (Hebrew chag shavū‘ot) and the day of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the church (Acts 2).
biblical_def: Pentecost is the great spring harvest festival of Israel and the day on which the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the New Testament church in fulfillment of Christ’s promise. Both meanings stand together in the Bible, the second fulfilling the first. The OT institution prescribed in Leviticus 23:15-21 commanded Israel to count seven complete weeks from the day after the Passover Sabbath (the day of the wave-offering of the firstfruits of the barley harvest), and on the fiftieth day to observe the Feast of Weeks (Hebrew chag shavū‘ot; Greek pentēkostē, fiftieth). Two loaves of leavened wheat bread were waved before the LORD, with sacrifices of seven lambs, one bullock, and two rams as burnt offerings, plus a kid for a sin offering and two lambs of the first year for a peace offering. The Feast of Weeks therefore celebrated the wheat harvest (the second great harvest of the year) and (in later Jewish tradition) the giving of the Law at Sinai, which was reckoned as having occurred fifty days after the Exodus. The New Testament fulfillment is on the day of Pentecost in Acts 2. The disciples, gathered in Jerusalem as Christ had instructed (Acts 1:4), are filled with the Holy Spirit; cloven tongues like as of fire sit upon each of them; they speak with other tongues as the Spirit gives them utterance; Peter preaches the great Pentecost sermon, the church receives the Spirit publicly, and three thousand souls are baptized into the church that day. The structural significance is enormous. First, the timing: the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost is theologically meaningful because the day was already the day of the wheat harvest’s firstfruits. The three thousand souls baptized at Pentecost are the firstfruits of the great gospel-harvest now beginning; James later calls believers a kind of firstfruits of his creatures (Jas 1:18). Second, the universalizing direction: the cloven tongues prefigure the going-forth of the gospel to every tongue and nation; the very list of nations in Acts 2:9-11 sets the missionary trajectory. Third, the new covenant inauguration: the Spirit’s indwelling of the church marks the formal arrival of the new covenant promised by the prophets (Jer 31:31-34; Ezek 36:26-27) in which the Spirit is poured out, the law written on hearts, and God’s people made one across every natural division. Fourth, the typological fulfillment: the OT Feast of Weeks anticipated the Day of Pentecost; the wheat-harvest firstfruits anticipated the Spirit-harvest firstfruits of three thousand souls; the giving of the Law at Sinai (in later Jewish tradition) is set against the giving of the Spirit at Pentecost (in the apostolic record). Pentecost is therefore the birthday of the New Covenant church in its Spirit-filled public manifestation, with the Spirit poured out upon all flesh in fulfillment of Joel 2:28-32, which Peter quotes in his sermon.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PENTECOST as a solemn festival of the Jews; so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day from the second day of the passover; also, the day on which the Holy Ghost descended upon the apostles, fulfilling the type of the OT Feast of Weeks.
webster_full: PENTECOST, n. — 1. A solemn festival of the Jews; so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day from the second day of the passover, which was the sixteenth of the month Nisan. The first day was set apart for receiving the sheaf of barley; on the morrow, the priest waved the sheaf before the LORD. From this day was reckoned the fiftieth, called the Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost. 2. Whitsuntide; the day on which the Holy Ghost descended upon the apostles, in fulfillment of the type of the OT Feast of Weeks (Acts 2).

corruption_summary: Pentecost is corrupted, on one side, by the disconnection of NT Pentecost from its OT typological roots (so that the Spirit’s outpouring is preached without the wheat-harvest firstfruits and Feast-of-Weeks substance the day already carried)—and on the other by the Pentecostal-traditions corruption that has treated Acts 2 as the normative template for ongoing personal Spirit-baptism experiences, against the apostolic doctrine that the once-for-all Pentecostal outpouring constituted the church and continues by indwelling rather than by repeated reception.
corruption_paragraphs: The disconnection of NT Pentecost from its OT typological roots is the more general contemporary corruption. The Spirit’s outpouring at Pentecost is preached without the wheat-harvest firstfruits substance, without the Feast-of-Weeks fiftieth-day-counting context, without the giving-of-the-Law-at-Sinai parallel that fills out the typology. The result is a Pentecost that hangs loose in Christian preaching, a one-time historical event with no rich OT substructure. The recovery is the recovery of the typology. Christ rose on the day after the Passover Sabbath (which was the day of the wave-offering of the firstfruits of barley); fifty days later, on the day already celebrated as the Feast of Weeks and the firstfruits of the wheat harvest, the Spirit was poured out and three thousand souls baptized as the firstfruits of the new covenant ingathering. The typological precision is the apostolic intent.

The opposite corruption is the Pentecostal-traditions reading of Acts 2 as the normative template for ongoing personal Spirit-baptism experiences—treating the day’s phenomena (tongues, fire, rushing wind) as the standard pattern by which every believer should experience subsequent Spirit-baptisms after conversion. The apostolic doctrine reads Acts 2 differently. The Pentecostal outpouring was the once-for-all constituting event by which the Spirit was given to the church as a body; subsequent believers receive the same Spirit at conversion through union with Christ (1 Cor 12:13, for by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body); the phenomena of Acts 2 are not normative for ongoing repeated experiences but constitutive of the church’s foundational reception of the Spirit. The continuing ministry of the Spirit is the indwelling, sealing, sanctifying, gifting work He performs in every believer from conversion onward, not a series of repeated Pentecost-style experiences. Recover both ends. Restore the OT typological substance of Pentecost (against the disconnection), and refuse the Pentecostal-traditions reading that turns the foundational event into a normative template (against the over-extension). The biblical Pentecost is the once-for-all outpouring that constituted the church; the Spirit continues His full ministry through indwelling, gifting, and applying to every believer the redemption Christ accomplished.

etymology: Firstfruits: the first-ripe portion of any harvest, offered to the LORD; Hebrew rē’shīth (first, beginning) or bikkūrīm (firstfruits). The OT feast prescribed in Leviticus 23:9-14, observed the day after the Passover Sabbath as the wave-offering of the first-ripe barley sheaf.
biblical_def: The Feast of Firstfruits was the second of the three great pilgrimage feasts of Israel (following Passover/Unleavened Bread) and the inaugurating event of the fifty-day count to Pentecost. Leviticus 23:9-14 prescribes the observance. On the day after the Sabbath of Passover week, the priest waved before the LORD a sheaf of the first-ripe barley harvest, accompanied by a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering, a meal offering of flour and oil, and a drink offering of wine. Until this wave-offering was made, no Israelite was to eat any of the new harvest’s bread, parched grain, or green ears—the firstfruits had to be presented to the LORD first, in acknowledgment that the whole harvest belonged to Him and was received as His gift. The structural significance of firstfruits in biblical theology is deep. First, the principle: the firstfruits represent the whole harvest. By presenting the first-ripe portion to the LORD, the offerer acknowledges that the whole crop is the LORD’s gift; what is given is the consecrating-portion that sanctifies the rest. Romans 11:16: for if the firstfruit be holy, the lump is also holy: and if the root be holy, so are the branches. Second, the typological fulfillment in Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 makes the doctrine explicit: but now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming. The risen Christ is the Firstfruits of the resurrection-harvest. He rose on the day after the Passover Sabbath—the exact day of the OT wave-offering of firstfruits—and His resurrection is the consecrating earnest of the great resurrection-harvest of His people at His return. Third, the ecclesial application: the church and believers are themselves named firstfruits. James 1:18: of his own will begat he us with the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures. Rom 16:5: Epaenetus is named the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ. 1 Cor 16:15: the household of Stephanas is the firstfruits of Achaia. Rev 14:4: the 144,000 are firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb. The firstfruits-category therefore extends across the canon: Israel as firstfruits to the LORD; Christ as Firstfruits of the resurrection; the church as firstfruits of God’s creatures; particular saints as firstfruits of their regions. Each instance preserves the principle: the firstfruits is the consecrating earnest, anticipating and guaranteeing the full harvest that follows.

corruption_summary: The firstfruits-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the prosperity-and-tithing-emphasis traditions that have reduced firstfruits to a fundraising principle (give the first-ripe of your income, and the LORD will bless the rest) without the deeper Christological and ecclesial substance the OT feast anticipates—and on the other by the general loss of typological reading that has dropped Christ-as-Firstfruits-of-the-resurrection from active preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-and-tithing-emphasis traditions have, in various forms, reduced firstfruits to a fundraising principle: give the first and best of your income to the LORD (or to His ministry, conveniently identified with the soliciting institution), and the LORD will bless what remains. There is a biblical pattern of firstfruits-giving from which this draws (Prov 3:9-10: honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine), but the principle is broader than fundraising and the substance is deeper than transactional return. The biblical firstfruits is the consecrating earnest that sanctifies the whole—and the supreme firstfruits is not the believer’s tithe but Christ’s resurrection, by which the whole resurrection-harvest of His people is sanctified and guaranteed. The recovery is the recovery of the doctrinal depth, with the practical principle of firstfruits-giving as one application of the broader theological substance, not the substance itself.

The general loss of typological reading has dropped Christ-as-Firstfruits-of-the-resurrection from active preaching in many traditions. Yet 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 makes the typology structural to the doctrine of the resurrection: Christ rose on the morrow after the sabbath (the exact day of the OT firstfruits wave-offering), and His resurrection is named the firstfruits of them that slept. The argument has enormous pastoral weight. The same Christ who rose is the Firstfruits whose resurrection consecrates and guarantees the resurrection of His people. The believer’s resurrection is not a vague hope but a covenantally-secured certainty, with Christ’s resurrection-firstfruits as its earnest. Where the typology is lost, the doctrine of bodily resurrection becomes a peripheral or even doubted teaching; where the typology is restored, the resurrection of the saints stands as firmly as the resurrection of Christ Himself, of which it is the harvest-conclusion. Recover both ends. Refuse the prosperity-reduction that flattens firstfruits to fundraising principle, and refuse the loss of typology that drops Christ-as-Firstfruits from the resurrection-doctrine. The biblical Feast of Firstfruits stands at the heart of the gospel’s resurrection-substance, with Christ’s rising on the day of the wave-offering of firstfruits as the consecrating earnest of every saint’s bodily resurrection at His return.

etymology: Trumpets: the silver trumpets and ram’s horn (shophar) blown to inaugurate the day. Hebrew yōm teru‘ah (day of blowing) or zīkhrōn teru‘ah (memorial of blowing); the OT festival prescribed in Leviticus 23:23-25, observed on the first day of the seventh month (Tishri 1; later called Rosh Hashanah).
biblical_def: The Feast of Trumpets was the OT festival inaugurating the seventh month (Tishri), the most sacred month of the Jewish religious year. Leviticus 23:23-25 prescribes the observance: in the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation. Ye shall do no servile work therein: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD. Numbers 29:1-6 adds detail on the burnt offerings and meal offerings. The day was marked by the blowing of trumpets (likely both the silver trumpets of Num 10 and the ram’s horn shophar); the cessation of ordinary work; the assembly of the people in holy convocation; and the offering of a young bullock, a ram, and seven lambs of the first year as burnt offerings, with the accompanying meal offerings and the daily and monthly sacrifices. The Feast of Trumpets inaugurated the most solemn ten-day period of the Jewish year, leading to the Day of Atonement on Tishri 10 and the Feast of Tabernacles beginning on Tishri 15. Later Jewish tradition came to call the Feast of Trumpets Rosh Hashanah (head of the year) and to associate it with the day of judgment and the heavenly opening of the books in which the year’s decrees are written—though these later associations go beyond the explicit OT specification. The typological substance of trumpets in biblical theology is extensive. Trumpets in Scripture sound at several great moments. The giving of the Law at Sinai was accompanied by the exceeding loud trumpet (Ex 19:16, 19; 20:18); the LORD’s coming-down to Sinai was marked by the trumpet of God. The trumpet calls Israel to war (Num 10:9). The trumpet announces the year of jubilee (Lev 25:9). The trumpet calls the assembly (Num 10:7). And in the New Testament, the trumpet is the apocalyptic signal of the Lord’s return. 1 Thessalonians 4:16: for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first. 1 Corinthians 15:52: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. Matthew 24:31: and he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds. The Feast of Trumpets therefore typologically anticipates the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return, which gathers His people, raises the dead in Christ, transforms the living, and inaugurates the consummation of redemption.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TRUMPET as a wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places; in scripture, the Feast of Trumpets (Lev 23:23-25) inaugurated the seventh month, typologically anticipating the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52).
webster_full: TRUMPET, n. — A wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places. In scripture, used for calling the assembly, for war, for the announcement of feasts, and (eschatologically) for the Lord’s coming.

FEAST OF TRUMPETS — A solemn festival of the Jews, observed on the first day of the seventh month, marked by the blowing of trumpets; the inauguration of the most sacred month of the Jewish year (Lev 23:23-25).

And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other.
corruption_summary: The Feast of Trumpets is corrupted, on one side, by the general loss of OT festal typology that has dropped its eschatological significance—and on the other by the speculative-date-setting tradition (especially in some dispensational and rapture-focused circles) that has attempted to pinpoint the rapture to the Feast of Trumpets in a specific year, against Christ’s explicit teaching that no man knoweth the day or hour.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of OT festal typology has dropped the Feast of Trumpets from contemporary preaching as obscure cultic detail without operative theological substance. The festival’s typological substance, however, is significant: trumpets in the biblical theology are the eschatological signal of the Lord’s great acts—the Law-giving at Sinai, the announcement of jubilee, the call to war, the gathering of the assembly, and ultimately the trumpet of the Lord’s return. The Feast of Trumpets sat at the head of the most solemn month of the Jewish year and anticipated the eschatological trumpet that would inaugurate the consummation. The recovery is the recovery of the typology. The trumpet of the Lord’s return is anticipated in the trumpets of Sinai, of Jericho, of jubilee, and of the seventh-month Feast of Trumpets; the saint listening for the eschatological trumpet hears it sounding from across the entire OT festal calendar.

The opposite corruption is the speculative-date-setting tradition that has, especially in some dispensational and rapture-focused circles, attempted to pinpoint the rapture to the Feast of Trumpets in a specific year. The reasoning typically goes: the rapture will involve a trumpet (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52); the Feast of Trumpets is the OT festival of trumpet-blowing; the typological connection suggests the rapture will occur on the Feast of Trumpets in a specific calendar year; therefore the date of the rapture is calculable. Christ Himself forecloses this entire reasoning: but of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only (Matt 24:36). The typological connection between the Feast of Trumpets and the eschatological trumpet is real; the inference to a specific date is forbidden. The recovery is the recovery of both: the typological substance (the Feast of Trumpets does anticipate the trumpet of the Lord’s coming) and the apostolic restraint (the date is not given to us, and speculation is not the right response). The Christian waits, watches, and prepares for the trumpet’s sound in faithful daily discipleship, not in date-setting speculation that Christ Himself forbade.

The Feast of Trumpets inaugurated the most sacred month of the Jewish year, leading to the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles.

etymology: New + moon; Hebrew chōdesh (new moon, month) from chādash (to be new); the first day of each month in the Jewish lunar calendar, marked by special offerings and the cessation of business in OT Israel.
biblical_def: The new moon (Hebrew chōdesh, both new moon and month) was a recurring monthly observance in OT Israel—the first day of each lunar month, marked by special offerings (Num 28:11-15), the blowing of trumpets (Num 10:10), the cessation of business (Amos 8:5), and the gathering of family for the new-moon feast (1 Sam 20:5, 18, 24-29). The Jewish calendar being lunar, the new moon was a visible monthly event, observed when the first sliver of the new crescent appeared in the western sky after sunset. The biblical doctrine of the new moon has several structural dimensions. First, the worship-and-offering function: the new moon was a time of special sacrifice. Numbers 28:11-15 prescribes two young bullocks, one ram, seven lambs of the first year for a burnt offering, with their meal offerings and drink offerings, plus a kid for a sin offering, in addition to the daily continual burnt offering. Each new month opened with a renewed dedication to the LORD. Second, the calendrical function: the new moon set the date for the various monthly observances. The Passover, Day of Atonement, Feast of Tabernacles, and other annual feasts were all dated relative to particular new-moon dates. The new-moon observance therefore served the calendrical infrastructure on which the rest of the festal year depended. Third, the prophetic-and-pastoral use: the new moon, together with the Sabbaths, appears in the prophets as marking the structured worship-life of Israel, often in contexts that warn against empty observance divorced from heart-religion. Isaiah 1:13-14: bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth. The LORD does not condemn the new moon as such (He instituted it); He condemns its observance by a people whose hands were full of blood. Fourth, the eschatological-and-NT register: Colossians 2:16-17 treats new moons together with the OT feast-days and sabbaths as shadows whose substance is Christ: let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. The new-moon observance, like the other OT calendar items, is fulfilled and superseded in the New Covenant by the Christ to whom it pointed. The eschatological echo is in Isaiah 66:22-23: for as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the LORD, so shall your seed and your name remain. And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD. In the new heavens and new earth, the worship of God continues in a rhythm that echoes the OT new-moon-and-sabbath calendar, with all flesh gathered to worship Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NEW MOON as the moon in its first visible crescent after conjunction with the sun; in scripture, the first day of each Hebrew lunar month, marked by special offerings and trumpet-blowing in OT Israel; with the other OT calendar items, treated by Paul as a shadow whose substance is Christ (Col 2:16-17).
webster_full: NEW MOON — The moon when it is in conjunction with the sun, and consequently invisible; or rather, the moon in its first visible crescent. Among the Jews, the first day of each lunar month, marked by special offerings (Num 28:11-15) and the blowing of trumpets (Num 10:10).
MOON, n. — The heavenly body which revolves round the earth, the second of the great lights of heaven (Gen 1:16); used in scripture for the marking of months and the festal calendar.
scriptures: Numbers 28:11
And in the beginnings of your months ye shall offer a burnt offering unto the LORD; two young bullocks, and one ram, seven lambs of the first year without spot.
Colossians 2:16-17
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Isaiah 1:13-14

Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; the new moons and sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting. Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth.
Isaiah 66:23
And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The new-moon observance is corrupted, on one side, by certain Hebrew-roots and Messianic movements that have urged Christian observance of the new-moon calendar as continuing covenantal obligation (against Col 2:16-17)—and on the other by the general loss of any sense of structured monthly worship-rhythm in much contemporary church life, leaving the calendar entirely shapeless beyond the weekly Lord’s Day.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew-roots and certain Messianic movements have, in various forms, urged Christian observance of the new-moon calendar as continuing covenantal obligation: Christians should mark the new moons, observe the feasts of Israel, return to the OT calendar as the structure of Christian worship. Paul explicitly rebukes this kind of imposition in Colossians 2:16-17, treating new moons together with feasts and sabbaths as a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. The OT calendar was the shadow; Christ is the substance; the New Covenant believer is not bound to observe OT new moons, feasts, and sabbaths as continuing covenantal obligations. The recovery is the recovery of the substance over the shadow: every new moon, every feast, every Sabbath has been fulfilled in Christ, and the New Covenant believer finds the substantive worship-reality of all the OT calendar items in his union with Christ and his ordinary Lord’s Day gathering.

The opposite corruption is the general loss of any sense of structured worship-rhythm in much contemporary church life. The Christian week, month, and year have become largely shapeless in many traditions: the weekly Lord’s Day remains (often diminished), but the monthly and annual rhythms that Christian tradition (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed) has variously preserved—the seasons of Advent, Lent, Easter, Pentecost; the saints’ days; the special providences’ commemorations—have been largely abandoned. Some abandonment is salutary (the medieval calendar had accumulated much that was unsubstantial); some is loss (the structured worship-rhythm of the Christian year has substantive pastoral value when ordered around Christ’s person and work). The Christian liberty to structure the calendar is real (Rom 14:5-6; Col 2:16); but the absence of any structure is its own loss. Recover both ends. Refuse the Hebrew-roots imposition of OT calendar items as continuing obligation, and refuse the shapeless un-rhythmic worship-life that has lost the value of structured Christian time. The biblical pattern is liberty in the particulars under the rule of the body of Christ: weekly Lord’s Day non-negotiable, annual rhythms wisely ordered around the gospel’s great events, and the believer’s worship-life shaped by patterns that point to Christ as the substance of every shadow.

etymology: Hebrew shabbāt, from shābat (to cease, rest); the seventh day of the week, established at creation as the day of God’s rest from His work and given to Israel as the perpetual sign of the covenant.
biblical_def: The Sabbath day is one of the foundational structural categories of biblical theology, established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, central to Israel’s covenantal life, fulfilled and re-anchored in Christ, and continuing under the New Covenant in the Christian Lord’s Day. The doctrine has several structural moments. First, creation. Genesis 2:2-3: and on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made. The Sabbath is grounded in the very order of creation, not merely in the Mosaic covenant; God Himself rested on the seventh day and sanctified it. Second, the Decalogue. Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15 set the fourth commandment: remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work... The Sabbath is grounded in the work-and-rest pattern of God Himself (Exodus version) and in the redemption from Egyptian slavery (Deuteronomy version). Third, the Mosaic covenant detail. The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel (Ex 31:13-17). Its violation is severe (Num 15:32-36). It is observed weekly, with cessation of ordinary labor for the household, servants, foreigners, and even animals (Ex 20:10). Fourth, the prophetic correction. The prophets repeatedly correct empty Sabbath-keeping (Isa 58:13-14) and condemn Sabbath-violation as covenant-breaking (Neh 13:15-22; Ezek 20). Fifth, the Christological fulfillment. Christ presents Himself as Lord even of the sabbath day (Mark 2:28); He corrects Pharisaic legalistic Sabbath-keeping; He performs healings on the Sabbath as proper works of mercy; He offers Himself as the One who gives true rest to the weary (come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, Matt 11:28). Hebrews 4 develops the theology: there remains a sabbath-rest for the people of God; entering the rest is by faith, not by works; the rest is finally consummated in the eschatological rest with God. Sixth, the New Covenant transposition. After Christ’s resurrection, the church gathered on the first day of the week (the Lord’s Day, Sunday, the day of the resurrection) for worship and the breaking of bread (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10). The historic Reformed tradition has understood this as the transposition of the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first—the perpetual moral substance of the fourth commandment (one day in seven set apart for worship and rest, grounded in creation) carried forward, with the specific day shifted to commemorate the resurrection. Some Reformed and almost all Lutheran traditions have understood the matter more loosely (the ceremonial-specific Sabbath of the Mosaic covenant fulfilled in Christ, with the Lord’s Day kept as the appointed Christian day of worship without the strict Sabbatarian application). Either way, the Christian honors the Lord’s Day as the appointed day of worship, finds his ultimate Sabbath-rest in Christ, and awaits the consummate Sabbath-rest in the new heavens and earth.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SABBATH as the day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employment, and to be kept holy and consecrated to His service and worship; established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, fulfilled in Christ, transposed to the Lord’s Day under the New Covenant.
webster_full: SABBATH, n. — 1. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employment, and to be kept holy and consecrated to His service and worship. 2. The day of the week appointed for the worship of God by Christians (the Lord’s Day or first day of the week); the Christian Sabbath. 3. Intermission of pain or sorrow; time of rest.

REST, n. — Cessation from motion or action of any kind; freedom from labor or exertion; in scripture, both the weekly rest of the Sabbath and the eschatological rest that remains for the people of God (Heb 4:9).
scriptures: Exodus 20:8-11
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work...
And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.
Hebrews 4:9-10
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.
Revelation 1:10
I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet.
corruption_summary: The Sabbath doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by Sabbatarian over-rigor that has often loaded the day with prohibitions the New Testament does not warrant and missed the rest-in-Christ substance (the Pharisaic pattern Christ rebuked, repeated in some strict Reformed traditions)—and on the other by the general contemporary collapse of any meaningful Lord’s Day observance, with Sundays now largely indistinguishable from other days in the lives of most Christians.
corruption_paragraphs: Sabbatarian over-rigor has been a recurring corruption across both Jewish and Christian history. The Pharisaic pattern Christ rebuked—loading the Sabbath with hundreds of detailed prohibitions, treating the day as legal-test more than rest-and-worship, missing the day’s purpose for refreshment and mercy-works—has been repeated in some strict Reformed traditions that have produced households exhausted by Sabbath-rigor rather than rested by Sabbath-grace. Christ’s corrective stands: the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath. The day is given for the worship of God and the refreshment of His people, not as a legalistic test loading the conscience with prohibitions. The recovery is the recovery of the day’s purpose—rest and worship in proper proportion—without the over-rigor that has often discredited Sabbath-keeping in the eyes of believers who experienced its legalistic distortion.

The opposite corruption is the general contemporary collapse of any meaningful Lord’s Day observance. Sundays in the lives of most contemporary believers are now largely indistinguishable from other days: church attendance for an hour or two, then back to ordinary work, shopping, entertainment, and the patterns of every other day. The structured one-day-in-seven set apart for worship and rest, which both Old and New Testament patterns assume, has been largely lost in most contemporary Christian practice. The cost is pastoral and personal: the believer who has no day-of-rest is the believer perpetually tired, perpetually distracted, perpetually without the structured worship-and-refreshment the Sabbath-pattern provides. The recovery is the recovery of Lord’s Day discipline: deliberate cessation from ordinary labor and commerce, deliberate prioritization of corporate worship, deliberate use of the day for spiritual refreshment, fellowship, family worship, and rest in Christ. The believer need not adopt strict Sabbatarian rigor (which can become its own bondage) to recover the substantial Lord’s Day pattern. The simple discipline of treating the Lord’s Day differently from the other days of the week—gathered worship as the day’s priority, ordinary commerce suspended, deliberate refreshment in the Lord and His people—restores much of what has been lost without the over-rigor that has discredited the doctrine.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabbāt (Sabbath, rest), from shābat (to cease); Greek sabbaton; the seventh-day weekly rest established at creation, codified in the Decalogue, fulfilled in Christ as Lord of the Sabbath, and transposed under the New Covenant to the Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection.

etymology: Weekly + Sabbath; distinguishing the seventh-day weekly Sabbath of the OT (and the Christian Lord’s Day under the New Covenant) from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts (e.g., the high Sabbath after Passover, the Sabbaths of the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles).
biblical_def: The weekly Sabbath is the recurring seventh-day Sabbath of Old Testament Israel, distinguished from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts (the high Sabbath after Passover; the Sabbaths of the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles; the Sabbatical Year; the Year of Jubilee). The distinction is structurally important because, while the various annual and septennial Sabbaths were ceremonial-specific to the Mosaic economy and have been fulfilled and superseded in Christ (Col 2:16-17), the weekly Sabbath is grounded in creation itself—and God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made (Gen 2:3)—and therefore stands as a creation ordinance distinct from the Mosaic ceremonial Sabbaths. The historic Reformed tradition has therefore made an important distinction: the Mosaic ceremonial Sabbaths (the annual feast-Sabbaths and the seventh-day specifically as Mosaic-ceremonial) are fulfilled in Christ and not binding on Christians; the weekly Sabbath-principle (one-day-in-seven set apart for worship and rest, grounded in creation and reaffirmed in the Decalogue’s grounding of the fourth commandment in the creation pattern) continues under the New Covenant, transposed to the Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection. The Lutheran and many Continental Reformed traditions have understood the matter somewhat differently, with less rigorous Sabbatarian application to the Lord’s Day; the Puritan-and-Presbyterian Reformed tradition has been more strict, treating the Lord’s Day with most of the weekly Sabbath’s discipline. The weekly Sabbath in the OT had several structural features. First, the cessation: ordinary work was to be suspended for the household, servants, foreigners, and even animals (Ex 20:10). Second, the worship: the Sabbath was a day of holy convocation (Lev 23:3), with the daily continual burnt offering doubled for the Sabbath (Num 28:9-10). Third, the redemption-remembrance: Deut 5:15 grounds the fourth commandment’s observance in the redemption from Egyptian slavery—the saint who rests on the Sabbath remembers that he was redeemed and therefore has a redeemed soul’s freedom to rest from labor. Fourth, the perpetual character: wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. It is a sign between me and the children of Israel for ever (Ex 31:16-17). The weekly Sabbath has therefore a creation-grounded substance that the New Covenant preserves under the Lord’s Day, with the specific day shifted and the ceremonial particulars of the Mosaic Sabbath fulfilled in Christ but the principle of one-day-in-seven worship-and-rest standing as a continuing creation-pattern for the people of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 distinguishes the weekly Sabbath (the seventh-day Sabbath grounded in creation) from the various annual Sabbaths of the Mosaic feasts; the former, by the historic Reformed tradition, continues under the New Covenant as the Christian Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection.
webster_full: WEEKLY SABBATH — The seventh-day Sabbath of OT Israel, grounded in creation (Gen 2:3) and the fourth commandment (Ex 20:8-11), distinguished from the various annual Sabbaths attached to feasts. Under the New Covenant, the principle continues in the Christian Lord’s Day (first day of the week) commemorating the resurrection of Christ.
SEVENTH-DAY, a. — Pertaining to the seventh day of the week; the day of the weekly Sabbath in OT Israel.

corruption_summary: The weekly Sabbath doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the seventh-day-Adventist tradition that has insisted on continued seventh-day (Saturday) Sabbath observance for Christians, against the New Testament pattern of first-day gatherings—and on the other by the antinomian-grace tradition that has dropped the weekly Sabbath-principle entirely, treating any day-of-rest as legalistic bondage, against the creation-grounded pattern that predates Moses and continues under the new covenant in the Lord’s Day.
corruption_paragraphs: The seventh-day-Adventist tradition (and certain other Sabbatarian movements) has insisted on continued seventh-day (Saturday) Sabbath observance for Christians, on the grounds that the fourth commandment specifies the seventh day specifically and that the church’s shift to the first day was a post-apostolic Roman corruption. The historic orthodox tradition refuses this reading. The shift from the seventh day to the first is apostolic, attested in the NT (Acts 20:7, breaking bread on the first day; 1 Cor 16:2, collection on the first day; Rev 1:10, the Lord’s Day), and theologically grounded in the resurrection. The creation-grounded substance of the weekly Sabbath (one-day-in-seven worship-and-rest) continues; the specific day is shifted to honor the resurrection-event by which Christ’s redemptive work was sealed. The recovery is the recovery of the historic orthodox position: the weekly Sabbath-principle continues under the New Covenant in the Lord’s Day, with the specific day-of-the-week appropriately shifted to commemorate the resurrection.

The opposite corruption is the antinomian-grace tradition that has dropped the weekly Sabbath-principle entirely, treating any day-of-rest as legalistic bondage from which Christian liberty has freed the believer. This reading misses the creation-grounded substance of the principle. The weekly Sabbath is not chiefly a Mosaic ceremonial item that has been fulfilled in Christ (though the specifically Mosaic particulars have been); it is a creation ordinance grounded in the very pattern of God’s own work-and-rest, given to all humanity (not Israel only) at the creation, and reaffirmed in the Decalogue’s grounding of the fourth commandment in the creation pattern. To drop the weekly Sabbath-principle is to lose a creation-grounded pattern that predates Moses and continues under the new covenant. The Christian liberty Paul defends in Romans 14:5-6 and Col 2:16-17 is liberty over the specific particulars of OT Sabbath-observance, not abolition of the principle of weekly worship-and-rest. Recover both ends. Refuse the Sabbatarian insistence on the seventh day against the apostolic Lord’s Day, and refuse the antinomian abandonment of any weekly Sabbath-principle. The biblical pattern is the weekly Lord’s Day as the creation-grounded, Christ-centered, gospel-shaped day of worship and rest for the New Covenant people of God.

etymology: Year + release; Hebrew sh’mīttāh, “release, letting-go”; the seventh year prescribed in Deut 15 in which Hebrew slaves were released, debts among Israelites were forgiven, and the land lay fallow.
biblical_def: The year of release was the seventh year of the seven-year cycle in OT Israel—a year of substantial covenantal-economic reset prescribed in Deuteronomy 15:1-18 and Leviticus 25:1-7. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the release of debts: at the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release. And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD’s release (Deut 15:1-2). Loans extended between Israelites were canceled in the seventh year; the lender had no further claim on the debtor for what had been borrowed. Loans to foreigners could be exacted (v. 3); the release was internal to the covenant community. Second, the release of Hebrew slaves: Deut 15:12-15 prescribes that a Hebrew bought into servitude for debt should serve six years, and in the seventh be released free. Moreover, the master was not to send him out empty but to furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress—a generous send-off acknowledging the LORD’s redemption of Israel from Egyptian slavery. Third, the fallowing of the land: Leviticus 25:1-7 prescribes that in the seventh year the land was to rest, with no sowing of the field, no pruning of the vineyard, no harvesting of what grew of itself for sale; the volunteer crops were to be the food of the household, the slave, the foreigner, and the animals alike. Fourth, the public reading of the law: Deut 31:9-13 prescribes that during the Feast of Tabernacles of the year of release, all Israel was to assemble before the LORD and hear the law read publicly. The year of release was therefore a comprehensive covenantal-economic-spiritual reset, in which the structures that had accumulated over six years (debt, servitude, agricultural strain) were unwound, the land rested, the people heard the law afresh, and the covenantal community was renewed. The typological substance is the gospel-pattern of release. The year of release prefigured the year of jubilee (the fiftieth year, after seven cycles of seven; Lev 25:8-17) and ultimately the gospel itself, which announces release to the captives (Luke 4:18-19, Christ’s reading from Isa 61 in the synagogue of Nazareth at the beginning of His ministry): The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord. The acceptable year of the Lord is the year of release inaugurated by Christ’s coming—the substantive release from the bondage of sin, the debt of guilt, the slavery of the curse—of which the OT seventh-year release was the typological shadow.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 treats RELEASE as the discharge from any obligation, claim, debt, or imprisonment; in scripture, the year of release (Deut 15) was the seventh year of the Hebrew cycle, in which debts were forgiven, Hebrew slaves were released, and the land lay fallow; typologically fulfilled in Christ’s announcement of the acceptable year of the Lord (Luke 4:18-19).
webster_full: RELEASE, n. — 1. A discharge from any obligation, claim, debt, or imprisonment. 2. In scripture, the year of release (Deut 15:1-2), the seventh year, when Hebrew creditors released their fellow-Israelites from debts and Hebrew slaves were set free; typologically anticipating the gospel’s release from the bondage of sin.

YEAR OF JUBILEE — The fiftieth year, after seven seven-year cycles, in which all sold land returned to its original family, all Hebrew slaves were freed, the land rested, and a great covenantal-economic reset occurred (Lev 25:8-17).

And when thou sendest him out free from thee, thou shalt not let him go away empty: Thou shalt furnish him liberally out of thy flock, and out of thy floor, and out of thy winepress...
corruption_summary: The year-of-release doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the general loss of OT economic-covenantal theology that has dropped its substantive teaching from contemporary preaching—and on the other by certain liberation-theology and contemporary debt-forgiveness movements that have read the year of release as a generic political program for cancellation of all debt, against the careful covenantal-community-internal scope of the OT prescription.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of OT economic-covenantal theology is the broader corruption that affects the year of release as it does the various OT economic provisions (gleaning, the kinsman-redeemer, the year of jubilee, the prohibition of interest among Israelites). These OT economic patterns are theologically rich, anchored in the LORD’s redemption of Israel from Egyptian slavery and pointing forward to the gospel’s great release of every soul from the bondage of sin. The contemporary preaching that skips them as obscure Mosaic detail misses the typological substance and the substantive principles of covenantal economic life the OT provides. The recovery is the recovery of the theological reading. The year of release is a creation-and-covenant-grounded structure of periodic economic reset within the covenant community, pointing typologically to the gospel’s great release from the bondage of sin that Christ inaugurates with His acceptable year of the Lord.

The opposite corruption is the liberation-theology and certain debt-forgiveness movements that have read the year of release as a generic political program for cancellation of all debt—urging modern states or international bodies to cancel the debts of poor countries on the model of the OT seventh-year release. The reading misses several features of the OT prescription. The release was internal to the covenant community: Hebrew creditors to Hebrew debtors. Loans to foreigners were not released (Deut 15:3). The release was an institutional structure within the LORD’s covenant with Israel, not a generic political ethic for any state to impose. The typological fulfillment is the gospel, which extends the substance of release universally—preach deliverance to the captives... preach the acceptable year of the Lord—but in the spiritual register of release from the bondage of sin, not as a political mandate for state-level debt cancellation. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of OT economic theology that drops the doctrine as obscure, and refuse the liberation-theology over-extension that reads the OT prescription as a generic political mandate. The biblical year of release is the typological shadow of which the gospel’s release-from-sin is the substantive fulfillment, with significant covenantal-community-economic principles for the church’s ordering of her own internal financial life under the gospel.

etymology: Meat in older English meant any food (not specifically flesh); the KJV uses meat offering for the Hebrew minōchāh, “tribute, present, grain offering,” which was actually a flour-and-oil grain offering, not a flesh sacrifice. Modern translations correctly render grain offering.
biblical_def: The meat offering of the KJV is the grain offering of modern translations—the Hebrew minōchāh, an offering of fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense, baked or fried into cakes or wafers, prescribed in Leviticus 2 and offered as an accompaniment to most of the other sacrifices. The KJV’s meat here is the older English word meaning food in general (compare green meat for vegetables, nutmeat for the edible kernel); modern English having narrowed meat to flesh of slaughtered animals, the KJV translation now misleads the modern reader. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the materials: fine flour (the staple food of life), oil (the substance of consecration and the Spirit’s anointing), frankincense (the substance of prayer ascending to the LORD), and salt (the substance of covenant—neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering, Lev 2:13). No leaven and no honey were to be used (Lev 2:11)—leaven typifying corruption-by-spread and honey typifying sweetness-without-substance. Second, the procedure: the offerer brought his offering to the priest, who took a memorial portion and burned it on the altar; the rest belonged to the priests as most holy of the offerings of the LORD made by fire (Lev 2:3). Third, the function: the meat offering typically accompanied the burnt offering and peace offering, not as a substitutionary atonement (the meat offering had no blood) but as an offering of devotion, tribute, and the firstfruits of the offerer’s labor. The flour and oil represented the offerer’s work (cultivation, harvest, milling, baking); the offering presented to the LORD the labor of the offerer’s hands as devoted to Him. Fourth, the typological substance. The meat offering with its no-leaven, no-honey, with-oil, with-salt particulars points toward Christ in His perfect humanity: fine flour without leaven (no corruption); anointed with oil (the Spirit without measure); seasoned with salt of the covenant (the unchanging fidelity to the Father’s purposes); offered without honey (no merely-sweet sentimentality but the substance of righteousness). Christ’s life of perfect devotion to the Father, offered as a continual minōchāh, is the substance the OT grain offering anticipated; and through Christ, the saint’s own labor and devotion are accepted before the LORD as a spiritual sacrifice well-pleasing to God (Heb 13:15-16; 1 Pet 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 notes that MEAT in older English denoted any food, and the KJV’s MEAT OFFERING is the Hebrew minōchāh, an offering of fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense, prescribed in Leviticus 2; modern translations correctly render grain offering.
webster_full: MEAT, n. — 1. Food in general; any thing eaten for nourishment, whether of man or beast. 2. The flesh of animals used as food. (The narrower modern sense.) 3. In scripture, the KJV uses meat offering for the Hebrew grain-and-flour offering (Lev 2).

OFFERING, n. — 1. The act of offering. 2. That which is offered; that which is presented in divine service. 3. In scripture, the various OT sacrifices and presentations to the LORD, including the burnt offering, peace offering, sin offering, trespass offering, meat (grain) offering, drink offering, and the like.
scriptures: Leviticus 2:1-2

And when any will offer a meat offering unto the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon: And he shall bring it to Aaron’s sons the priests: and he shall take thereout his handful of the flour thereof, and of the oil thereof, with all the frankincense thereof; and the priest shall burn the memorial of it upon the altar...
Leviticus 2:11
No meat offering, which ye shall bring unto the LORD, shall be made with leaven: for ye shall burn no leaven, nor any honey, in any offering of the LORD made by fire.
Leviticus 2:13

And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.
Hebrews 13:15-16

By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
corruption_summary: The meat-offering doctrine is corrupted primarily by the KJV-translation drift in modern English: meat no longer means food generally but specifically flesh, so the modern reader of the KJV encounters meat offering and forms an incorrect picture (a flesh offering rather than a grain offering)—and by the general loss of typological reading that has dropped the meat/grain offering from contemporary preaching as obscure ritual detail.
corruption_paragraphs: The KJV-translation drift is the most concrete contemporary corruption of the meat-offering doctrine. Meat in 1611 English meant food in general; meat offering was therefore a perfectly natural rendering of the grain-and-oil-and-frankincense offering Leviticus prescribes. In modern English, meat has narrowed to flesh of slaughtered animals, with the result that the modern reader of the KJV forms an incorrect picture: a flesh offering rather than the grain offering Scripture actually describes. The remedy is partly translational (modern translations have correctly rendered grain offering) and partly catechetical (KJV readers should be taught that meat in the KJV often means food generally, as in strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age in Heb 5:14, which clearly means strong food, not strong flesh). The KJV’s antique vocabulary is rich and rewarding but requires this kind of careful attention to the language-shift over four centuries.

The deeper corruption is the general loss of typological reading that has dropped the meat/grain offering from contemporary preaching as obscure ritual detail without typological substance. The grain offering, with its no-leaven (no corruption), no-honey (no merely-sweet sentimentality), oil (the Spirit’s anointing), and salt (the covenant’s fidelity) particulars, typifies Christ in His perfect humanity and the substance of His life of devotion to the Father. The recovery is the recovery of the typology: the OT sacrifices were the appointed shadows of which Christ is the substance; the grain offering particularly points to the substance of Christ’s perfect humanity offered in devotion to the Father, and to the spiritual sacrifices of praise and good works the saint now offers through Him (Heb 13:15-16). The contemporary preacher who skips Leviticus 2 misses one of the more pastorally tender of the OT typologies; the recovery of typological reading restores the doctrinal substance and the spiritual application alike.

etymology: High + Sabbath; the KJV phrase at John 19:31 (that sabbath day was an high day) for a Sabbath that coincided with one of the annual feast-days, making it doubly sacred; Greek megalē hēmera, “great day.”
biblical_def: The high Sabbath in biblical usage is a Sabbath that coincides with one of the annual feast-days, making it a doubly-sacred day in the Jewish calendar. The phrase appears explicitly in John 19:31 of the Sabbath following Christ’s crucifixion: the Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. The Sabbath following Christ’s death was a high Sabbath because it fell during Passover week—specifically, it was the Sabbath of the Feast of Unleavened Bread (the first day of which, Nisan 15, was itself a high-day Sabbath, regardless of which day of the week it fell on; the regular weekly Sabbath that year coincided with the feast-week, doubling the sanctity of the day). Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the categorical distinction. OT Israel had two kinds of Sabbaths: the weekly Sabbath (every seventh day, regardless of season) and the annual feast-day Sabbaths (the first day of Unleavened Bread, the day after the Passover Sabbath, the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, the first day of Tabernacles, and the eighth day of Tabernacles—each of these annual feast-days was itself a Sabbath in the sense of being a day of cessation from ordinary work and holy convocation, but not necessarily falling on the seventh day of the week). The annual Sabbaths could land on any day of the week, and when one of them coincided with the weekly seventh-day Sabbath, the day was doubly sacred: a high Sabbath. Second, the chronological significance for Christ’s death. The high Sabbath of John 19:31 has implications for the chronology of the crucifixion-and-resurrection. Many traditional readings have held that Christ was crucified on Friday and rose on Sunday; some careful chronological readings have argued that the high Sabbath of John 19:31 indicates a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion (with the high Sabbath being the annual Sabbath of the first day of Unleavened Bread, not the weekly Saturday), allowing for the three-days-and-three-nights of Matt 12:40. The chronological details are contested, but the recognition of high Sabbaths as a category distinct from weekly Sabbaths is structurally important for the reading. Third, the broader typological substance. The high Sabbath as a doubly-sacred day—weekly Sabbath plus annual feast-Sabbath—points to the consummate sacred-time of the new heavens and earth, where the rest of the eternal Sabbath is also the rest of the consummated feast (the marriage supper of the Lamb, the gathering in the heavenly city) in one perpetual high-Sabbath that brings both rhythms together forever. The categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths therefore matters not only chronologically but theologically: the New Covenant believer’s ultimate rest is the consummate high Sabbath where the weekly and annual rhythms meet in eternal worship of the Lord at His feast.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 treats SABBATH as the day of rest; the high Sabbath of John 19:31 is the doubly-sacred Sabbath that coincides with an annual feast-day, making the day doubly holy in the Jewish calendar.
webster_full: HIGH SABBATH — A Sabbath day that coincides with one of the annual feast-days of the Jewish calendar, making it doubly sacred. For that sabbath day was an high day (John 19:31).

FEAST-DAY, n. — A day appointed for some particular religious celebration; in OT Israel, the annual feast-days (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, etc.), each of which had its own appointed Sabbath of rest, distinct from the weekly seventh-day Sabbath.
scriptures: John 19:31

The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
Leviticus 23:7-8

In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein. But ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD seven days: in the seventh day is an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein.
Matthew 12:40
For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
Revelation 19:9
And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God.
corruption_summary: The high-Sabbath doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of the categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths, which produces confused readings of the crucifixion chronology (forcing all Sabbath-references in John 19 onto the weekly seventh-day Sabbath when the high Sabbath was actually the annual feast-day Sabbath)—and by the consequent loss of the typological richness of the consummate high Sabbath of the new heavens and earth.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of the categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths is the broader corruption that affects the high-Sabbath doctrine. Contemporary readers, accustomed to thinking of the Sabbath as exclusively the weekly seventh-day Sabbath, force every Sabbath-reference in the Gospels onto the weekly Saturday, missing the annual feast-day Sabbaths that the OT explicitly establishes (Lev 23) and that the Jewish first-century calendar uniformly preserved. The high Sabbath of John 19:31 is one specific example: a Sabbath that was an high day precisely because an annual feast-Sabbath coincided with the weekly Sabbath (or because the annual feast-Sabbath was itself the day in question, depending on the chronological reading). The recovery is the recovery of the categorical distinction: OT and first-century Jewish Sabbaths included both weekly seventh-day and annual feast-day, and the careful reading of the Gospels’ chronology requires attention to which kind was operative in any given passage.

The typological substance of the high Sabbath as a doubly-sacred day points toward the consummate sacred-time of the new heavens and earth, where the weekly-Sabbath-rhythm of God’s ordered worship and the annual-feast-rhythm of the redemptive-historical celebrations meet in one perpetual eternal-Sabbath that is also the consummated wedding-feast of the Lamb. The loss of this typological substance is part of the broader loss of OT festal typology that has impoverished contemporary preaching. The recovery restores not only the chronological precision (for example, the careful reading of the resurrection-week sequence) but also the doctrinal-and-pastoral substance: the saint’s ultimate rest is the consummate high Sabbath of eternal worship at the marriage supper of the Lamb in the new heavens and earth, where every weekly Lord’s Day and every annual gospel-commemoration finds its substantive eschatological fulfillment in one perpetual high day before the throne.

Loss of the categorical distinction produces confused chronological readings; recovery restores both the precise chronology and the typological substance of the consummate high Sabbath of the new heavens and earth.
